en.title: Physiotherapy: the whole course
en.short: What physiotherapy is, how the degree is organised, its main areas and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach physiotherapy concepts to students. They are not medical advice, and they do not replace supervised teaching, textbooks or official guidelines. They give no drug doses. Clinical guidelines change and differ between countries, so check the current national guidance or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance. Physiotherapy involves touching and moving people, so practise only under supervision and with consent. If someone is unwell or in crisis, they should seek local medical help.

sections.heading: What physiotherapy is
sections.text: Physiotherapy, also called physical therapy in many countries, is a health profession that helps people move, function and take part in daily life. It uses exercise, education, manual techniques, physical agents and assistive technology. It serves people with pain, injury, surgery, neurological disease, heart and lung conditions, and developmental or age-related problems. It works in hospitals, clinics, homes, schools, sports settings and communities. The profession values patient-centred care, consent, safety, evidence and teamwork. Its history includes exercise and massage traditions, but modern practice is based on anatomy, physiology, movement science and research. Scope of practice is set by each country’s law and regulator, so it varies.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text: The degree has different names and lengths. In Nigeria, physiotherapy is usually a university degree, often awarded as BPT or BSc Physiotherapy; graduates must complete a supervised internship and register with the Medical Rehabilitation Therapists Board of Nigeria to practise. Confirm the current award, duration and internship rules with your school and regulator. In the United Kingdom, the usual route is a three-year BSc (Hons) Physiotherapy or a two-year pre-registration MSc; registration with the Health and Care Professions Council is required to practise. In the United States, entry is now usually at doctoral level, the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT), followed by state licensure. Other countries differ. Programmes often start with basic sciences, then assessment and treatment principles, then clinical placements. Always check your own handbook for modules, hours and assessment.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text: Teaching usually moves in stages. The introduction covers the profession, its history, scope and values; musculoskeletal anatomy; nervous system and visceral anatomy; exercise physiology; biomechanics and kinesiology; motor control and movement science; pathology, inflammation and tissue healing; pain science; and communication and patient education. The core stage covers physiotherapy assessment and clinical reasoning, then principles of exercise therapy, manual therapy, electrotherapy and physical agents. Clinical modules follow: musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiopulmonary, paediatric, geriatric, sports and women’s health physiotherapy. Community rehabilitation and health promotion, assistive technology and mobility, professional ethics and law, and research methods and evidence-based practice run alongside. At master’s level, advanced modules deepen musculoskeletal, neuro and cardiorespiratory rehabilitation, and a research methods module supports a dissertation. The order can vary, but foundations before clinical practice is common.

sections.heading: How to study physiotherapy
sections.text: Learn anatomy and physiology by linking structure to function and to a real movement, such as standing up from a chair. Draw joints, nerves and muscles from memory. For each condition, ask what is damaged, how it heals, what the person cannot do, and which treatment aims to change that. Practise assessment in pairs under supervision: consent, safety, observation, testing and recording. Use case examples with African settings and names, but remember that resources differ. Test yourself with short questions and spaced revision rather than rereading. Watch demonstrations, then explain the reasoning aloud. Read one current guideline or review for each major area and note its country and date. Keep a reflective log of what you saw and what you would do differently.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text: Students often memorise treatment lists without assessment findings, so they cannot justify a choice. Others treat a diagnosis, such as stroke, as if every patient were the same. Some forget consent, dignity, infection control and safety, or they give exercise without checking technique, pain response and fatigue. In written work, students may quote one country’s guideline as universal or ignore the date. Another mistake is to read only notes and never handle anatomy models, patients or equipment. Finally, do not diagnose or treat yourself, family or friends from these notes. Clinical decisions need a qualified clinician who can assess the person directly.

keyPoints: Physiotherapy helps people move, function and take part in daily life through exercise, education, manual therapy, physical agents and assistive technology.
Physiotherapy degrees differ by country in name, length and registration; check your own handbook and national regulator.
Study foundations first, then assessment and treatment principles, then clinical areas.
Link anatomy and physiology to real movement and to each patient’s activity limits.
Practise only under supervision, with consent, safety and dignity.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice; guidelines change, so check current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Physiotherapy as a profession: history, scope and values
en.short: What physiotherapy is, its history, scope, values, teamwork and regulation.

sections.heading: What physiotherapy is
sections.text: Physiotherapy, called physical therapy in some countries, is a health profession concerned with human movement and function. Physiotherapists assess movement and function, plan care, deliver treatment and promote health. They use exercise, manual therapy, education and physical agents such as heat, cold and water. Scope covers prevention, treatment and rehabilitation across the lifespan, from children to older adults. Physiotherapists work in hospitals, clinics, community services, sport, schools and workplaces. In some countries they are first-contact practitioners, meaning patients can see them without a doctor’s referral; national rules decide this.

sections.heading: History and growth
sections.text: Modern physiotherapy grew in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries from massage, exercise and hydrotherapy. Rehabilitation after war and polio epidemics expanded the profession. Associations formed to set standards, and the international confederation is World Physiotherapy, formerly the World Confederation for Physical Therapy. Training moved into universities in many countries.

sections.heading: Values and teamwork
sections.text: Core values include patient-centred care, evidence-based practice, safety, dignity, equity and accountability. Patient-centred practice starts from the person’s goals and respects autonomy, consent, culture and confidentiality. The physiotherapist explains findings, agrees goals and checks understanding. Teamwork matters: physiotherapists refer and share records with doctors, nurses, occupational therapists, speech therapists and community health workers. Roles must be clear, and the person remains central. For example, Amina, a market trader in Ibadan, attends with knee pain. The physiotherapist explains the assessment, asks what matters to her, agrees a goal of walking to market, and works with the nurse and community health worker. Amina gives consent and may refuse.

sections.heading: Regulation and bodies
sections.text: Regulation varies by country. Many countries require registration or licensure, protect the title, set a code of conduct and require continuing professional development. Professional bodies represent members and promote standards. In Nigeria, for example, the Medical Rehabilitation Therapists (Registration) Board of Nigeria registers physiotherapists, and the Nigeria Society of Physiotherapy is the professional association; check current rules with official sources. Always check the national regulator where you practise.

keyPoints: Physiotherapy is a health profession concerned with movement, function and daily activity.
Its modern roots lie in massage, exercise, hydrotherapy and rehabilitation after war and polio.
Scope spans prevention, treatment and rehabilitation across the lifespan and many settings.
Core values include patient-centred care, evidence-based practice, safety, dignity and equity.
Consent, shared goals and clear teamwork are central to patient-centred practice.
Regulation and professional bodies vary by country; check the national regulator.

en.title: Musculoskeletal anatomy for physiotherapy
en.short: Bones, joints, muscles, tendons and ligaments of the limbs, spine and pelvis, plus surface landmarks.

sections.heading: Bones and landmarks
sections.text: Anatomy is the study of body structure. In the musculoskeletal system, bones form the skeleton and act as levers for movement, protect organs and store minerals. A landmark is a named bony point you can feel. In the anatomical position the body stands upright, palms forward. Common landmarks include the acromion, olecranon, anterior superior iliac spine, iliac crest, greater trochanter, patella, tibial tuberosity, medial malleolus and lateral malleolus. The spine has cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal regions. The pelvis links the spine to the lower limbs.

sections.heading: Joints and range
sections.text: A joint is where bones meet. Fibrous and cartilaginous joints allow little or no movement; synovial joints have a capsule, synovial fluid and cartilage and allow most limb movement. Range of motion is the amount of movement at a joint, measured in degrees with a goniometer, an angle-measuring instrument. It depends on joint shape, capsule, ligaments, muscles and pain. Reference ranges vary with age, sex, body build and method, so use local reference values. The shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints; the elbow and knee are hinge-type joints.

sections.heading: Muscles, tendons, ligaments
sections.text: A muscle produces force by contracting. Its action is the movement it causes at a joint, such as flexion or extension. The agonist is the prime mover, the antagonist opposes it, and a synergist assists. A tendon attaches muscle to bone and transmits force. A ligament attaches bone to bone and stabilises the joint. Muscles can act at more than one joint, so their action depends on line of pull and joint position. Palpation means feeling structures through the skin. Palpate with consent, compare both sides and begin with bony landmarks.

sections.heading: Surface anatomy case
sections.text: Amina, a football player, has knee pain. The physiotherapist palpates the patella, tibial tuberosity and joint line, and asks her to straighten the knee against resistance to feel the quadriceps. This shows how anatomy guides examination. It does not replace full assessment or diagnosis. Clinical practice and local rules vary, so follow your programme and current national guidance.

keyPoints: Bones act as levers, protect organs and provide palpable landmarks.
Synovial joints allow most limb movement; range is measured in degrees and varies between people.
A tendon joins muscle to bone; a ligament joins bone to bone.
The agonist is the prime mover, the antagonist opposes it and a synergist assists.
Palpate with consent, compare both sides and start with bony landmarks.
Anatomy guides examination but does not replace diagnosis; follow local guidance.

en.title: Nervous system and visceral anatomy
en.short: Nervous system organisation, dermatomes, myotomes, reflexes, cranial nerves and the thoracic and pelvic viscera.

sections.heading: Organisation of the nervous system
sections.text:
The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system (PNS) links it to the body. The somatic part carries sensation and drives voluntary muscle. The autonomic part controls smooth muscle, heart and glands: sympathetic for fight or flight, parasympathetic for rest and digestion.

Damage above the anterior horn cell gives an upper motor neuron pattern (raised tone, brisk reflexes); damage to the cell or axon gives a lower motor neuron pattern (weakness, wasting, reduced reflexes).

sections.heading: Dermatomes, myotomes and reflexes
sections.text:
A dermatome is the skin area supplied by one spinal nerve root; a myotome is the muscle group that root mainly supplies. Landmarks: C6 thumb, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral border of foot. Myotomes: C5 shoulder abduction, C6 wrist extension, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, S1 plantarflexion.

A reflex is an automatic response to a stimulus; the knee jerk is L3-L4 and the ankle jerk S1. Maps vary slightly between textbooks.

sections.heading: Cranial nerves
sections.text: Twelve pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain and brainstem: I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal, VI abducens, VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory, XII hypoglossal. For physiotherapy, the vagus (X) matters for swallow, voice and cough; the facial nerve (VII) for eye closure; the accessory nerve (XI) for trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. New swallowing difficulty raises aspiration risk; check before oral feeding.

sections.heading: Thoracic and pelvic viscera
sections.text:
The thorax holds the lungs, pleura, heart and mediastinum, separated from the abdomen by the diaphragm. The abdomen holds the liver, stomach, intestines, kidneys and spleen; the pelvis holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs. Visceral pain is poorly localised and may be felt in a skin area sharing the same spinal segment, called referred pain.

Case: after abdominal surgery a student reports right shoulder tip pain. The diaphragm is supplied by C3-C5, the same segments as the shoulder, so irritation refers pain there.

keyPoints: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; the PNS links it to the body, with somatic and autonomic parts.
Upper motor neuron lesions raise tone and reflexes; lower motor neuron lesions cause weakness, wasting and reduced reflexes.
A dermatome is the skin area of one spinal root; a myotome is the muscle group it supplies.
Landmarks: C6 thumb, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral border of foot.
The knee jerk is L3-L4 and the ankle jerk S1; compare both sides.
The diaphragm is supplied by C3-C5, so diaphragm irritation can refer pain to the shoulder tip.

en.title: Physiology of exercise and training response
en.short: Cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic, endocrine and heat responses, plus fatigue, recovery and fitness.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular and respiratory
sections.text:
Exercise raises oxygen demand. Cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) rises, and blood flow shifts to working muscle. Breathing deepens and speeds up, mainly through larger tidal volume (air per breath), so ventilation matches carbon dioxide production. VO2max is the highest oxygen uptake in large-muscle exercise.

Example: at rest 70 beats/min × 70 mL = 4.9 L/min; during exercise 140 × 100 mL = 14 L/min. Values vary. Training raises stroke volume, so a given workload needs a lower heart rate.

sections.heading: Metabolic and endocrine
sections.text:
Muscles regenerate ATP (adenosine triphosphate, the cell’s energy currency) by three systems: phosphocreatine for seconds, glycolysis (glucose breakdown) for short high-intensity work, and oxidative phosphorylation for longer work. Glycolysis can produce lactate, but lactate is a fuel, not simply the cause of fatigue.

Adrenaline and noradrenaline raise heart rate and mobilise glucose and fat. Cortisol and growth hormone support fuel supply and repair. Insulin falls during exercise while glucagon rises. Responses vary with intensity, duration, fitness and environment.

sections.heading: Heat, fatigue and recovery
sections.text:
Working muscles make heat. Thermoregulation increases skin blood flow and sweating; evaporation cools the body. High humidity reduces evaporation and raises heat risk.

Fatigue is a fall in performance from fuel depletion, metabolic changes, heat and central nervous factors. Recovery restores fluid and glycogen, allows tissue repair, and includes sleep. Needs differ between people.

sections.heading: Fitness principles
sections.text: Physical fitness includes cardiorespiratory endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. Training follows overload, specificity, progression, reversibility and individuality. Overload means stressing the body above its usual load; specificity means adapting to the exact demand; progression means increasing gradually; reversibility means gains fade when training stops; individuality means responses differ between people. Clinical exercise advice should follow current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, and it rises during exercise.
Ventilation increases mainly through larger tidal volume and higher breathing frequency.
ATP is regenerated by phosphocreatine, glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.
Lactate is a fuel, not simply the cause of fatigue.
Thermoregulation uses skin blood flow and sweating; high humidity reduces evaporation.
Training follows overload, specificity, progression, reversibility and individuality.

en.title: Biomechanics and kinesiology: forces, levers and human movement
en.short: Forces, levers, torque, centre of mass, joint motion, posture and gait in human movement.

sections.heading: Forces, levers and torque
sections.text:
Biomechanics applies mechanics to living tissue; kinesiology studies human movement. A force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N). Gravity, muscle tension and ground reaction are common forces. A lever is a rigid segment turning about a fulcrum. Bones are levers and joints are fulcrums. First-class levers have the fulcrum between load and effort; second-class have the load between; third-class have the effort between. Most limb levers are third class, favouring speed over force.

Torque is the turning effect of a force: torque = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, the moment arm. Example: a 50 N load acts 0.30 m from the elbow. Torque = 50 × 0.30 = 15 N m. A muscle at 0.20 m needs 15 ÷ 0.20 = 75 N to balance it. Centre of mass is the point where body mass balances; stability improves when it lies within a wider base of support.

sections.heading: Joint kinematics and kinetics
sections.text:
Kinematics describes movement without forces: displacement, velocity and acceleration. Joint kinematics includes range of motion and angular velocity. Kinetics explains movement by forces and torques. Newton’s laws apply: a muscle torque produces angular acceleration, while gravity and load resist it.

A force plate measures ground reaction force in walking, with vertical, anterior-posterior and mediolateral parts. These ideas help assess loading and movement quality.

sections.heading: Posture and gait
sections.text:
Posture is the alignment of body segments against gravity. Good posture needs low effort and balanced load, not one rigid shape. Gait is walking. The gait cycle has stance, when the foot is on the ground, and swing, when it moves forward.

Step length is the distance between successive contacts of opposite feet; stride length is two steps. Cadence is steps per minute. Mechanical analysis examines joint angles, torques and ground reaction forces. It helps explain limping, fatigue and falls. Clinical decisions follow current local assessment guidance.

keyPoints: Biomechanics applies mechanics to living tissue; kinesiology studies human movement.
A force is a push or pull in newtons; a lever turns about a fulcrum.
Torque = force × perpendicular moment arm, measured in N m.
Worked check: 50 N × 0.30 m = 15 N m; at 0.20 m the balancing force is 15 ÷ 0.20 = 75 N.
Kinematics describes motion; kinetics explains it by forces and torques.
Centre of mass within the base of support aids stability; gait has stance and swing phases.

en.title: Motor control and movement science
en.short: How the nervous system controls posture, balance and skilled movement, and what this means for rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Control of movement
sections.text: Motor control is how the nervous system plans, starts, adjusts and stops movement. The cortex plans and initiates voluntary action. The basal ganglia help select and scale movements, and the cerebellum coordinates timing and corrects errors. Brainstem and spinal circuits organise posture and reflexes. Muscles, joints and skin send sensory information back to these centres. Skilled movement is not a fixed programme; the nervous system predicts what will happen and adjusts as it goes.

sections.heading: Posture and balance
sections.text: Posture is the alignment of body parts against gravity. Balance is control of the body’s centre of mass over its base of support. The nervous system combines vision, vestibular input from the inner ear and somatosensory input from skin, joints and muscles. It then uses feedforward control, preparing for a predicted disturbance, and feedback control, correcting after sensory error. Balance responses include ankle, hip and stepping strategies. A person may feel steady yet still have poor balance under changed conditions.

sections.heading: Development and learning
sections.text: Motor development is the change in movement ability across life. It follows broad sequences, such as head control before sitting and walking, but timing varies between children. Motor learning is a lasting change in the ability to perform a skill, produced by practice and experience. Practice works best when it is task-specific, varied and suitably challenging. Feedback can be knowledge of results, information about the outcome, or knowledge of performance, information about the movement itself. Feedforward develops as the learner predicts the task.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation implications
sections.text: Rehabilitation applies these ideas through task-specific practice. A therapist sets a goal that matters to the person, gives clear cues, and adjusts difficulty so errors are useful but not overwhelming. For example, Amina, after a stroke, practises standing from a chair. The therapist changes seat height, adds a reaching task and gives feedback on knee position. Practice is repeated and later tested in a new setting. This builds feedforward control and transfer, not only strength. Local guidelines vary; check national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Motor control is how the nervous system plans, starts, adjusts and stops movement.
Posture is alignment against gravity; balance keeps the centre of mass over the base of support.
Vision, vestibular and somatosensory input support balance through feedforward and feedback control.
Motor development follows broad sequences but timing varies; motor learning is a lasting change from practice.
Feedback uses sensory information about the outcome or the movement; feedforward predicts the movement in advance.
Task-specific, varied practice with useful feedback supports rehabilitation and transfer.

en.title: Pathology, inflammation and tissue healing
en.short: Cell injury, inflammation, repair in key tissues, and healing delays that guide physiotherapy timing.

sections.heading: Cell injury and inflammation
sections.text: Pathology is the study of disease processes. Cell injury may be reversible or irreversible. Irreversible injury causes necrosis, uncontrolled cell death that triggers inflammation; apoptosis is programmed death with little inflammation. Acute inflammation is the early response to injury or infection. It has five classic signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. Blood vessels widen and leak, then white cells arrive. Neutrophils come first, followed by macrophages. Inflammation clears debris and prepares repair, but prolonged inflammation can damage tissue.

sections.heading: Repair and tissue healing
sections.text: Repair happens by regeneration, replacing cells of the same type, or by fibrosis, forming scar. Granulation tissue, new vessels and collagen, fills the gap. Collagen is then remodelled and becomes stronger with controlled loading. Tissues differ. Muscle can regenerate after minor injury but forms scar after large tears. Tendon heals slowly because it has poor blood supply, and collagen must align along load. Bone heals through a callus, a bridge of new bone, or by direct healing when well stabilised. Cartilage has poor blood supply and limited regeneration, so defects often fill with fibrocartilage, a scar-like cartilage. A peripheral nerve can regrow after Wallerian degeneration, breakdown of the nerve fibre beyond the injury, if the cell body is intact and the gap is small; growth is slow and varies.

sections.heading: Delays and physiotherapy timing
sections.text: Healing is delayed by poor blood supply, infection, smoking, poor nutrition, uncontrolled diabetes, age, and some medicines such as corticosteroids. Excessive movement can disrupt repair, but too little movement causes stiffness and weak tissue. Physiotherapy timing therefore matches the healing stage. Early on, protect the tissue and control pain while keeping nearby joints moving. Later, add graded loading and functional exercise as repair allows. For example, Amina, a student with a quadriceps strain, begins gentle isometric contractions, muscle tightening without length change, and protected walking, then progresses to resisted exercise when pain and swelling settle. Local protocols and current national or WHO guidance should guide care.

keyPoints: Reversible cell injury can recover; irreversible injury causes necrosis and inflammation.
Acute inflammation has five signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function.
Repair occurs by regeneration or fibrosis, and collagen remodelling strengthens scar tissue.
Muscle, tendon, bone, cartilage and nerve heal at different rates and with different limits.
Poor blood supply, infection, smoking, poor nutrition, diabetes and some medicines delay healing.
Physiotherapy timing should match the healing stage, with protection early and graded loading later.

en.title: Pain science for rehabilitation
en.short: Nociception, sensitisation, referred pain, the biopsychosocial model and pain assessment in rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Nociception and pain
sections.text:
Nociception is the nervous system’s encoding of noxious stimuli. Nociceptors are free nerve endings that respond to heat, pressure or chemicals. Nociception is not pain.

Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience produced by the brain when it judges that the body needs protection. A person can have tissue damage without pain, or pain without new tissue damage.

sections.heading: Sensitisation and referred pain
sections.text:
Peripheral sensitisation means nociceptors become more responsive after injury. Inflammatory chemicals lower their threshold, so normal movement may hurt. Central sensitisation means neurons in the spinal cord and brain amplify pain signals. It produces hyperalgesia, which is more pain from a painful stimulus, and allodynia, which is pain from a non-painful stimulus.

Referred pain is felt away from its source. Visceral and somatic nerves converge on the same spinal neurons, so the brain wrongly attributes the signal to a body region.

sections.heading: Biopsychosocial model
sections.text:
The biopsychosocial model says pain and disability are shaped by biological, psychological and social factors. Biological factors include tissue injury and sensitisation. Psychological factors include fear, worry and beliefs about pain. Social factors include work, family, income and access to care.

The model does not say pain is imaginary. It explains why two people with similar scans can have different pain and function.

sections.heading: Assessment and rehabilitation
sections.text:
Pain assessment records location, quality, timing, intensity and effect on function. Use a simple scale, such as 0 to 10, and ask what makes pain worse or better. Screen for red flags, which are signs of serious disease, and yellow flags, which are psychological or social risks for persistent pain.

Rehabilitation combines pain education, graded activity, pacing and goal setting. For example, Amina, a 24-year-old trader in Kano, has low back pain after lifting. Her scan is normal but she fears movement. The physiotherapist explains sensitisation, agrees small walking goals and increases activity gradually. Her fear and disability fall. Guidelines differ by country and change, so check current national guidance.

keyPoints: Nociception is the encoding of noxious stimuli; pain is a brain-produced experience.
Peripheral sensitisation makes nociceptors more responsive after injury.
Central sensitisation amplifies signals and causes hyperalgesia and allodynia.
Referred pain is felt away from its source because of convergence in the spinal cord.
The biopsychosocial model shows that biological, psychological and social factors shape pain.
Assessment seeks red flags, yellow flags and functional impact; rehabilitation uses education, graded activity and pacing.

en.title: Communication and patient education
en.short: Communication skills, active listening, patient education, adherence and working with interpreters and families.

sections.heading: Core communication skills
sections.text: Communication in physiotherapy is more than giving instructions. It is a two-way exchange that builds trust and supports shared decisions. Useful skills include open questions such as 'What worries you most?', active listening, empathy, summarising and checking non-verbal cues. Active listening means giving full attention, reflecting back what you heard and asking clarifying questions. Use silence and allow time to answer. Avoid jargon, and confirm consent and privacy before sensitive discussions.

sections.heading: Explaining and teaching
sections.text: Patient education is planned teaching that helps a person understand their condition and take part in managing it. Explain in plain language, in small chunks, and check understanding with teach-back: ask the person to explain the plan in their own words. Say what physiotherapy can and cannot do, and that progress and guidelines vary by country and case. For example, Amina, a trader in Kano with knee osteoarthritis, is shown how exercise may reduce pain and improve walking. The physiotherapist asks her to demonstrate the home plan and say what she will do on a bad day.

sections.heading: Adherence and interpreters
sections.text: Adherence is the extent to which a person follows an agreed plan. It is not the same as obedience. Adherence is shaped by understanding, beliefs, cost, transport, family support and how the plan fits daily life. Ask about barriers without blaming, agree goals, and simplify the plan where possible. Adherence is a partnership, not a test of the patient. Family members can help, but involve them only with the person’s consent and protect confidentiality. When language differs, use a trained interpreter, not a child. Speak to the patient, keep sentences short, avoid jargon, and check understanding. Current national professional guidance and World Health Organization (WHO) resources should be checked because advice changes.

keyPoints: Communication is a two-way exchange; use open questions, active listening and summarising.
Teach-back checks understanding by asking the patient to explain the plan in their own words.
Adherence means following an agreed plan and is shaped by practical and personal barriers.
Ask about barriers without blaming and agree shared goals.
Family members need the patient’s consent, and confidentiality must be protected.
Use trained interpreters rather than children, and check current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Physiotherapy assessment and clinical reasoning
en.short: History, observation, palpation, movement and neurological tests, outcome measures and clinical reasoning.

sections.heading: History and observation
sections.text: Assessment begins with history taking: the patient’s story of the main problem, onset, aggravating and easing factors, previous episodes, health, medicines, work, home and goals. Assessment is not medical advice; local rules and current national or World Health Organization guidance apply. Observation means looking before touching: posture, gait, swelling, redness, scars, muscle wasting and movement. Compare both sides and record what you see.

sections.heading: Physical examination
sections.text: Palpation uses the hands to assess temperature, tenderness, swelling and tissue texture. Range of motion (ROM) is the movement available at a joint, measured in degrees with a goniometer. Muscle testing grades strength, often from 0 to 5, where 5 is normal against resistance. Neurological screening checks sensation, reflexes, power and nerve-related symptoms. Select tests to confirm or refute early ideas, not as a routine list.

sections.heading: Reasoning and measures
sections.text: Clinical reasoning is the thinking that turns findings into a hypothesis, a testable explanation that guides the next question or test. Outcome measures are standard tools, such as patient-reported questionnaires or timed walking tests, used at the start and end to show change. Choose one that fits the person and problem, and record the score. Case: Amaka, a trader in Enugu, has knee pain after a fall. History and observation suggest a knee problem; palpation and ROM localise it; muscle testing and neurological screening check other causes. Her problem list might read: reduced knee ROM, weak quadriceps, pain limiting walking. The plan follows these findings and her goal to return to market work.

sections.heading: Problem list and plan
sections.text: A physiotherapy problem list states the impairments, activity limits and participation restrictions you will address. It is not a medical diagnosis. The plan sets goals, treatment, review dates and what would make you change course. Share it with the patient and team. If symptoms are severe, worsening or unexplained, refer for medical review. Guidelines differ between countries and change, so check current national or World Health Organization guidance.

keyPoints: History taking and observation come before physical tests and guide what to examine.
Palpation, range of motion, muscle testing and neurological screening are selected to test a hypothesis, not used as a routine list.
Clinical reasoning turns findings into a testable hypothesis and then into a problem list.
Outcome measures are standard tools used at the start and end to show change.
A problem list describes impairments, activity limits and participation restrictions, not a medical diagnosis.
Guidelines differ by country and change, so check current national or WHO guidance and refer when symptoms are severe or unexplained.

en.title: Principles of exercise therapy
en.short: How to prescribe exercise safely: FITT, progression, regression, adherence and training types.

sections.heading: Prescription framework
sections.text: Exercise therapy is planned physical activity used to restore function and reduce disability. The FITT principle sets Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time or duration (how long) and Type (what kind). Good prescription is individualised to the person’s condition, goals and fitness. It follows specificity (training must match the goal), overload (the body adapts only when stressed above its usual level) and reversibility (gains are lost if training stops). Intensity can be set by rating of perceived exertion (RPE, a 0 to 10 scale of effort), heart rate, or a percentage of one-repetition maximum (1RM, the heaviest load lifted once with good form).

sections.heading: Aerobic and strength
sections.text: Aerobic training uses large muscle groups in rhythmic activity, such as walking or cycling. It improves endurance. Intensity is often guided by the talk test or RPE; heart-rate targets are estimates and vary with age and medicines. Strength training uses resistance to improve force. A common prescription is sets of repetitions at a percentage of 1RM. For example, if a person’s 1RM leg press is 40 kg, then 70% 1RM is 0.70 × 40 = 28 kg. Flexibility training uses controlled stretches held for a short time to improve range. Functional training practises tasks the person needs, such as sit-to-stand or stair climbing.

sections.heading: Progression and safety
sections.text: Progression increases one variable at a time, usually load or repetitions, when the person tolerates it. Regression reduces load, volume or complexity during pain, fatigue or illness. Adherence improves with clear goals, education, self-monitoring and a programme that fits daily life. Safety requires screening, checking current national or World Health Organization guidance, and stopping if chest pain, severe breathlessness or dizziness occurs. A small case: Amina, a teacher with knee osteoarthritis, starts with short daily walks and sit-to-stand practice; her physiotherapist reviews pain and function before increasing time.

keyPoints: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type.
Specificity, overload and reversibility explain why training must match the goal and be maintained.
Intensity can be set by RPE, heart rate or a percentage of 1RM; for example, 70% of a 40 kg 1RM is 28 kg.
Progression increases one variable at a time; regression reduces load or volume when needed.
Adherence is supported by clear goals, education and self-monitoring.
Safety needs screening, current national or WHO guidance, and stopping if warning symptoms occur.

en.title: Principles of manual therapy
en.short: Passive movement, mobilisation, manipulation, massage and traction: mechanisms, safety, contraindications and limited evidence.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.text: Manual therapy is hands-on treatment by a trained therapist. Passive movement is movement produced by the therapist while the patient relaxes. Mobilisation uses graded passive movements, often oscillatory, within the available range or at its limit. Manipulation is a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, often beyond the patient’s active control. Massage is manual soft-tissue manipulation. Traction applies longitudinal force to separate joint surfaces, manually or mechanically.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and uses
sections.text: Proposed mechanisms include mechanical effects on joint motion and tissue, nerve-related pain modulation such as gate control (reduced pain signalling in the spinal cord) and descending inhibition (brain control of pain), and contextual effects from touch, reassurance and expectation. These are plausible but not fully established. Manual techniques are used as an adjunct for musculoskeletal pain, stiffness, restricted range and soft-tissue tightness. They should support exercise, education and self-management, not replace them.

sections.heading: Safety and contraindications
sections.text: Screen for red flags (warning signs) before treatment: suspected fracture or dislocation, infection, malignancy in the area, unstable spine, severe osteoporosis and acute inflammatory arthritis. Do not treat without consent. Massage is avoided over open wounds, burns, infection and suspected deep vein thrombosis. Traction is avoided in unstable spine, spinal cord compression, acute fracture and infection. Neck (cervical) manipulation needs extra caution because rare serious vascular events have been reported; use it only with training and current national guidance. Record consent, reassess after treatment and report adverse events.

sections.heading: Evidence and case
sections.text: Systematic reviews find small, short-term benefits for some neck and low back pain, but evidence is limited and often low quality. Effects are similar to exercise or other active care. An audible pop does not prove success. Adverse events include soreness and bruising, and rarely serious injury. Case: Chidi, a 30-year-old office worker in Lagos, has neck stiffness without red flags. After assessment and consent, the therapist uses gentle mobilisation and massage, teaches exercise and reassesses. Manipulation is not used because it is not clearly indicated.

keyPoints: Passive movement is produced by the therapist; mobilisation is graded passive movement; manipulation is a high-velocity thrust.
Manual therapy is an adjunct, not a cure, and should be combined with exercise and education.
Screen for red flags and obtain consent before any hands-on technique.
Massage is avoided over open wounds, infection and suspected deep vein thrombosis; traction is avoided in unstable spine and cord compression.
Evidence is limited: small short-term benefits for some musculoskeletal pain, similar to active care.
An audible pop does not prove successful manipulation.

en.title: Electrotherapy and physical agents
en.short: Safe use of heat, cold, ultrasound, electrical stimulation and laser in physiotherapy.

sections.heading: Principles and effects
sections.text: Physical agents are controlled forms of energy applied to the body: heat and cold (thermal), ultrasound (acoustic), electrical stimulation, and laser (light). They aim to change pain, inflammation, circulation, muscle activity or tissue repair. Heat causes vasodilation, relaxation and pain relief. Cold causes vasoconstriction, reduced swelling and analgesia. Ultrasound uses sound waves and can produce thermal and nonthermal effects. Electrical stimulation excites nerves or muscles; TENS is used for pain and NMES for muscle activation. Laser therapy uses light, often at low level, and its effects and evidence vary. Dose depends on intensity, duration, area and frequency, so follow the device instructions and local protocols.

sections.heading: Safety and contraindications
sections.text: Assess before use: diagnosis, skin, sensation, circulation, implants, pacemaker, pregnancy, cognition and medicines. Contraindications differ by agent. Many texts list impaired sensation, poor circulation, active bleeding, infection and some malignancies as cautions or contraindications; check the specific device and local policy. For electrical stimulation, avoid current across the heart and use caution with pacemakers and pregnancy. For heat, avoid prolonged use over numb or poorly supplied skin. For cold, avoid cold hypersensitivity and Raynaud’s phenomenon. For ultrasound, avoid eyes, heart and pregnant uterus. For laser, protect the eyes. Infection control includes hand hygiene, clean skin, cleaning reusable electrodes and probes as the manufacturer directs, single-use items where required, and safe waste disposal. Electrical safety includes inspecting leads, turning intensity to zero before applying, and stopping if pain or skin change occurs.

sections.heading: Case and evidence
sections.text: Case: Amina, 64, has knee osteoarthritis. A short warm pack before exercise may ease stiffness, but check her skin and sensation, keep the temperature comfortable and inspect the skin afterwards. If she had a pacemaker, electrical stimulation near the chest would need specific advice. Evidence for each agent varies, and guidelines change. Check current national guidance and, where relevant, World Health Organization guidance. This summary is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: Physical agents are controlled thermal, acoustic, electrical or light energy used to change pain, circulation, muscle activity or healing.
Heat causes vasodilation and relaxation; cold causes vasoconstriction and analgesia.
TENS is used for pain and NMES for muscle activation; electrical current across the heart is avoided.
Check sensation, circulation, skin, implants, pacemaker and pregnancy before applying any agent.
Contraindications differ by agent, so follow the device instructions and local policy.
Clean equipment and hands, and use single-use items where required to prevent infection.

en.title: Musculoskeletal physiotherapy: assessment and conservative care
en.short: Assessment and conservative care for spine and limb conditions, using exercise, manual therapy and self-management.

sections.heading: Assessment and screening
sections.text: Musculoskeletal physiotherapy assesses pain, function and participation. History covers onset, aggravating and easing factors, morning stiffness, trauma, work and sleep. Physical examination tests movement, strength, joint range and special tests. Use validated outcome measures, such as a pain scale and a condition-specific function score, to record change. Screen for red flags before treating: unexplained weight loss, fever, night pain, neurological deficit, bladder or bowel changes, or recent serious trauma. These need medical review. Most low back pain is nonspecific, meaning no serious cause is found, and routine imaging is not usually needed without red flags. Guidelines differ by country and change, so check current national or World Health Organization guidance.

sections.heading: Exercise and manual therapy
sections.text: Exercise is the main conservative treatment. It may be strengthening, aerobic, range-of-movement or motor control work. Progress load gradually and make it specific to the person’s goals. Manual therapy means skilled passive movement, such as mobilisation or manipulation. It can reduce pain briefly and improve movement, but it is an adjunct, not a cure. Explain this honestly. Self-management includes education, activity modification, home exercise and goal setting. Encourage the person to return to ordinary activity as able.

sections.heading: Common conditions
sections.text: Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis of joint pain and stiffness, often with activity-related pain. Exercise, weight management when relevant and education are core. Tendinopathy is a tendon problem with load-related pain and reduced function; progressive loading is central. Low back pain is usually managed with reassurance, staying active and exercise. Post-fracture rehabilitation is guided by the stage of healing and surgeon instructions: protect the repair, then restore movement, strength and function.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Consider Amina, a market trader with knee osteoarthritis. Assessment records pain on walking, stair difficulty and a function score. Care includes a home strengthening plan, advice to keep active, and review of load. Manual therapy may be added briefly for pain relief. Reassess function after some weeks. This is an educational example, not individual medical advice.

keyPoints: Screen for red flags before treating and refer for medical review when present.
Most low back pain is nonspecific, and routine imaging is not usually needed without red flags.
Exercise is the main treatment, manual therapy is an adjunct, and self-management supports recovery.
Osteoarthritis care combines exercise, education and weight management when relevant.
Tendinopathy is load-related, and progressive loading is central.
Post-fracture rehabilitation protects healing first, then restores movement, strength and function.

en.title: Neurological physiotherapy
en.short: Assessment and rehabilitation for adults with stroke, spinal cord injury, Parkinson’s disease and multiple sclerosis.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.text: Neurological physiotherapy helps adults with damage or disease of the nervous system to improve or maintain function. Assessment begins with history, goals and examination. After stroke, record side affected, sensation, vision, cognition, tone, power, balance and walking. Tone is resistance to passive movement; it may be high (hypertonia) or low. For spinal cord injury, define the neurological level and completeness using the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury, and check breathing, skin, bladder and bowel. In Parkinson’s disease, note bradykinesia (slowness), rigidity, tremor, freezing and falls. In multiple sclerosis, note relapses, fatigue and heat sensitivity. Use valid outcome measures and record activity. Check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Task-specific training
sections.text: Rehabilitation is active and goal-directed. Task-specific training means practising the real task, such as standing up, stepping or reaching, not only moving one muscle. Repetition and gradual progression matter. Balance training challenges sitting, standing and stepping while support is reduced. Gait training may use cueing, a walking aid or body-weight support. In Parkinson’s disease, external cues such as counting and large-amplitude movements can help. In multiple sclerosis, plan around fatigue and heat. Tone is assessed, but lowering tone is not the only aim; positioning and active movement often improve function.

sections.heading: Function and participation
sections.text: Functional independence means doing daily tasks with as little help as possible. Set goals with the person. In spinal cord injury, teach transfers, wheelchair skills, pressure relief and bladder care; standing or walking depends on the level and completeness of injury. After stroke, practise dressing, washing and walking in the real setting. In Parkinson’s disease and multiple sclerosis, include falls prevention, dual-task practice where safe, and energy conservation. A 62-year-old man after stroke has a weak left leg and poor standing balance. He practises sit-to-stand with a frame, then stepping; progress is checked by the time to stand five times and by walking speed. Check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Assessment records impairment, activity limitation, participation and the person’s goals, using valid measures.
Task-specific training practises real tasks with repetition and graded progression.
Balance and gait training should be challenging but safe, with support reduced as ability improves.
In Parkinson’s disease, external cues and large-amplitude movement can improve walking; in multiple sclerosis, plan around fatigue and heat.
Tone is resistance to passive movement; lowering tone is not the only aim of rehabilitation.
Functional independence is doing daily tasks with as little help as possible; check current national or WHO guidance because protocols change.

en.title: Cardiopulmonary physiotherapy
en.short: Breathing exercises, airway clearance, exercise testing and cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Breathing and clearance
sections.text: Cardiopulmonary physiotherapy helps people with breathlessness, sputum retention and poor exercise capacity. Breathing exercises teach relaxed breathing, pursed-lip breathing (a slow breath out through pursed lips) and diaphragmatic breathing. They can ease breathlessness and anxiety, but they do not replace medical treatment. Airway clearance techniques move sputum: active cycle of breathing techniques (ACBT), autogenic drainage (breathing at different lung volumes to move sputum), postural drainage, positive expiratory pressure (PEP) and oscillating devices. Choice depends on the condition, sputum load, fatigue and preference. For example, Amina, a student with bronchiectasis and a wet cough, is taught ACBT with huffing (a forced breath out with an open throat) after assessment. If she feels dizzy or her oxygen saturation falls, she stops and staff follow the local protocol.

sections.heading: Exercise testing
sections.text: Exercise testing measures the body’s response to effort. Common tests are the six-minute walk test, which records the distance walked in six minutes, the incremental shuttle walk, and the cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET), which measures oxygen uptake and ventilation. Record heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation (SpO2), breathlessness and fatigue before, during and after. Stop for chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness, unsafe ECG changes or a fall in SpO2 as defined by the local protocol. Testing guides rehabilitation and helps assess risk; it does not give a diagnosis on its own.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation and safety
sections.text: Cardiac rehabilitation combines supervised exercise, education, risk-factor care and support after a heart attack, after procedures to restore blood flow, or in stable heart failure. Pulmonary rehabilitation is a supervised exercise and education programme for people with chronic lung disease, especially chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), who remain breathless. Programmes are individualised and progress gradually. Monitor symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2 and perceived exertion, using a scale such as Borg. Have emergency plans and trained staff. This is education, not medical advice. Guidelines change and differ by country; check current national cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation guidelines and international statements, such as those from the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society, and World Health Organization rehabilitation guidance.

keyPoints: Breathing exercises such as pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing can ease breathlessness but do not replace medical treatment.
Airway clearance techniques include ACBT, autogenic drainage, postural drainage, PEP and oscillating devices; choose by assessment and local protocol.
Exercise tests include the six-minute walk test, incremental shuttle walk and CPET; record heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2 and symptoms.
Stop exercise testing for chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness, unsafe ECG changes or a fall in SpO2 as defined locally.
Cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation combine supervised exercise, education and risk-factor or self-management support.
Guidelines differ by country and change; check current national and international sources such as ATS/ERS statements and WHO guidance.

en.title: Paediatric physiotherapy
en.short: Child development, family-centred assessment and play-based therapy for childhood movement conditions.

sections.heading: Typical development
sections.text:
Child development is the gaining of gross motor, fine motor, language, cognitive and social skills. The sequence is predictable, but timing varies. Head control comes before sitting, sitting before standing, and standing before walking.

Fine motor control moves from whole-hand grasp to a thumb-and-finger grasp. Language moves from cooing and babbling to words and short sentences. Play moves from solitary to parallel and cooperative play. Physiotherapists look for loss of skills, persistent asymmetry, unusual tone or delayed milestones, and check concerns against current national guidance.

sections.heading: Family-centred assessment
sections.text:
Family-centred assessment puts the child and caregivers at the centre. The physiotherapist takes a history of pregnancy, birth, illness and concerns; observes play and daily routines; and assesses muscle tone, strength, posture, movement and participation. Goals are agreed with the family as activities the child needs to do, such as sitting to eat.

Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from an early brain lesion. The Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) grades gross motor function in cerebral palsy from I to V. Physiotherapy aims at strength, mobility, participation and comfort, and prevention of contractures (fixed shortening). Developmental delay means slower progress in one or more domains; early stimulation and coaching are better than waiting. Congenital (present at birth) and neuromuscular disorders need plans for positioning, movement, respiratory care and mobility aids. Guidelines differ by country and change, so follow national or World Health Organization guidance.

sections.heading: Play and caregivers
sections.text:
Play is the child’s main way of learning. Play-based therapy uses toys, songs, games and routines to practise movement, balance and hand use. Caregivers are partners: they learn handling, positioning, safe stretching and how to weave practice into feeding, bathing and play.

Case: Amina, aged three, has cerebral palsy and cannot sit steadily. Her therapist coaches her mother to support her with a firm chair and rolled cloth at meals, and to play a reaching game daily. They review progress and adjust the plan together.

keyPoints: Development follows a general sequence, but the timing varies between children.
Family-centred assessment includes history, observation, muscle tone and movement, participation and agreed goals.
Cerebral palsy is non-progressive; physiotherapy targets function, comfort and prevention of contractures.
Developmental delay needs early stimulation and coaching, not a wait-and-see approach.
Play-based therapy uses toys, songs and routines to practise movement and hand use.
Caregivers are partners; teach handling, positioning and safe home practice, and follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Geriatric physiotherapy
en.short: Ageing, frailty, falls, osteoporosis, dementia and multimorbidity, with exercise and rehabilitation for older adults.

sections.heading: Ageing and frailty
sections.text: Ageing brings gradual loss of muscle mass, strength and bone density, and decline in balance, but older adults are very different from one another. Frailty is a clinical syndrome of low reserve, so a small stress such as infection or a fall can cause disproportionate decline. It is not the same as disability or simply being old. Sarcopenia means loss of muscle mass and strength. Physiotherapy aims to preserve function, independence and confidence, not only to treat disease.

sections.heading: Falls and osteoporosis
sections.text: Falls usually have several causes: muscle weakness, poor balance, vision problems, foot pain, cognitive impairment, medicines and home hazards. Falls prevention combines strength and balance training, review of medicines and vision, home safety and education. Osteoporosis is low bone mass with damaged bone structure, which raises the risk of fragility fracture, a break after a minor fall. Weight-bearing and resistance exercise can help bone and muscle, but must be tailored to fracture risk and pain. Check current national or World Health Organization guidance.

sections.heading: Dementia and multimorbidity
sections.text: Dementia affects memory, learning and judgement, so teaching must be simple, repeated and supported by carers. Exercise can improve mobility and mood and may reduce falls, but programmes need supervision and routine. Multimorbidity means two or more long-term conditions. It changes priorities: fatigue, pain, depression and polypharmacy, meaning many medicines, interact. Goals should be person-centred, realistic and shared with the family and team.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation approach
sections.text: Rehabilitation in older adults is function-focused. A physiotherapist assesses mobility, transfers, balance, strength and falls risk, then sets goals such as walking to the toilet safely. A case: Mrs Adeyemi, 78, has knee osteoarthritis, hypertension and mild cognitive impairment. After one fall she fears walking. The plan includes seated-to-standing strength work, supervised balance practice, a walking stick, home hazard changes, vision and medicine review, and carer education. Progress is reviewed and the plan adjusted.

keyPoints: Frailty is a syndrome of reduced reserve, not the same as old age or disability.
Falls are multifactorial, so prevention combines strength and balance training with medicine, vision and home review.
Osteoporosis raises fragility fracture risk; exercise must be tailored to the person.
Dementia care needs simple, repeated teaching and carer support.
Multimorbidity requires person-centred goals and review of many medicines.
Check current national or WHO guidance because protocols vary.

en.title: Sports physiotherapy
en.short: Preventing injury, managing acute injuries, rehabilitation, return to sport and working with coaches.

sections.heading: Prevention and load
sections.text: Sports physiotherapy helps active people train and compete with less risk of injury. Injury prevention combines screening, technique and conditioning, and load management. Load is the total stress from training and competition: volume, intensity and frequency. A sudden rise in load, poor recovery or a new movement pattern can raise injury risk. The aim is not to avoid all load but to progress it gradually and monitor the athlete’s response. Strength, balance, mobility and sport-specific skills are built over time. Follow current national or sport governing body guidance, because screening and prevention programmes differ.

sections.heading: Acute injury management
sections.text: An acute injury happens suddenly, such as a sprain or muscle strain. First, protect the area and screen for serious problems: deformity, severe swelling, loss of sensation, or inability to bear weight need urgent assessment. Early management aims to limit bleeding and swelling, control pain and preserve safe movement. Relative rest, ice, compression and elevation are commonly taught, but details vary, so use local first-aid guidance. Avoid harmful massage or vigorous stretching early. Refer when needed and record findings.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation and return
sections.text: Rehabilitation is a planned programme to restore movement, strength, control and confidence. It moves from pain control and gentle movement to strength, power, agility and sport-specific drills. Return to sport is a decision, not a single day. Criteria usually include little or no pain, full movement, strength near the other side, passed functional tests and psychological readiness. A case: Ada, a college basketball player with an ankle sprain, progresses from walking and balance to hopping and cutting only when these criteria are met. The physiotherapist shares the plan with the coach.

sections.heading: Strength and teamwork
sections.text: Strength and conditioning uses progressive overload, meaning gradually increasing demand, and specificity, meaning training resembles the sport. Individualise the plan and include recovery. The physiotherapist works with coaches, strength staff and the athlete: agree goals, roles and communication, and document decisions. Clear teamwork reduces the chance of conflicting advice and premature return.

keyPoints: Sports physiotherapy aims to reduce injury risk while allowing gradual, monitored training load.
Acute injury care begins with protection, screening for serious injury and local first-aid guidance.
Rehabilitation progresses from movement and pain control to strength, power and sport-specific skills.
Return to sport uses shared criteria such as pain, movement, strength, functional tests and readiness.
Strength and conditioning apply progressive overload and specificity, individualised to the athlete.
Physiotherapists, coaches and athletes should agree goals, roles and communication and document decisions.

en.title: Women’s health physiotherapy
en.short: Pelvic floor function, pregnancy and postnatal physiotherapy, incontinence, pelvic pain and respectful referral.

sections.heading: Pelvic floor and continence
sections.text:
The pelvic floor is a group of muscles, mainly levator ani and coccygeus, with fascia. It supports the bladder, uterus and rectum, helps control urine and faeces, and contributes to sexual function. A healthy floor contracts at effort and relaxes to pass urine or stool. Symptoms are common but not inevitable.

Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) means repeated, supervised contractions. It is a common first-line treatment for stress and mixed urinary incontinence in women; bladder training helps urgency. Faecal incontinence may improve with PFMT, bowel habit advice and referral. Internal assessment is done only with consent, after explanation, in private, with a chaperone offered.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and postnatal care
sections.text:
Antenatal physiotherapy teaches safe exercise in pregnancy, posture, pelvic floor training and preparation for birth. Exercise should be adjusted to the person; stop and seek advice for bleeding, fluid loss, chest pain, severe breathlessness or painful contractions. National and World Health Organization (WHO) antenatal guidance should be checked because advice varies.

Postnatal physiotherapy supports recovery, pelvic floor training, gradual return to activity and abdominal wall recovery. Pelvic floor training should be taught correctly and reviewed. Screen for urinary and faecal incontinence, pelvic pain and mood concerns, and refer when needed.

sections.heading: Pelvic pain and referral
sections.text:
Pelvic pain includes pelvic girdle pain, pain with intercourse and bladder or bowel pain. Physiotherapy uses education, exercise, relaxation and manual therapy where appropriate. Respectful assessment means explaining each step, gaining consent, offering a chaperone, using trauma-informed language and taking distress seriously rather than treating it as normal.

Refer for red flags such as suspected infection, malignancy, neurological symptoms, postpartum complications or persistent pain. Document findings and share information only with consent, except where safety or the law requires. Case: Amina, 28 weeks pregnant, leaks urine when coughing. A physiotherapist teaches PFMT and bladder habits, checks technique, and refers if pain or bleeding appears.

keyPoints: The pelvic floor supports pelvic organs and helps control urine and faeces; PFMT is supervised pelvic floor muscle training.
PFMT is a common first-line treatment for stress and mixed urinary incontinence in women, and bladder training helps urgency.
Antenatal exercise advice must be individualised and checked against current national and WHO guidance.
Postnatal physiotherapy supports pelvic floor recovery, gradual return to activity and screening for incontinence and pelvic pain.
Respectful pelvic assessment requires explanation, consent, privacy and a chaperone.
Refer red flags such as suspected infection, malignancy, neurological symptoms or postpartum complications.

en.title: Community rehabilitation and health promotion
en.short: Community-based rehabilitation, disability inclusion, home programmes and health promotion in local health systems.

sections.heading: Community-based rehabilitation
sections.text: Community-based rehabilitation (CBR) is a strategy for rehabilitation, equal opportunity and social inclusion of people with disabilities. It combines the efforts of disabled people, families, communities and health, education, livelihood and social services. The WHO CBR Guidelines (2010) group activities into health, education, livelihood, social and empowerment. CBR is not a cheap clinic service; it builds local participation and links people to mainstream services. Low-resource programmes may use community workers, peer groups and local materials.

sections.heading: Disability and inclusion
sections.text: The WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) describes disability through body functions and structures, activities, participation, and environmental and personal factors. Disability is not only a body problem; steps, transport, attitudes and policies can exclude people. Inclusion means taking part in school, work, worship and community life with needed support. Physiotherapists should ask about these barriers, and respect the person’s goals and consent.

sections.heading: Home programmes and promotion
sections.text: Home-based programmes train a family member or caregiver in safe practice, such as positioning, daily tasks and simple equipment. The physiotherapist teaches, checks technique and reviews progress; the family is not left alone. Health promotion aims to enable people to increase control over their health. The Ottawa Charter (WHO, 1986) names five areas: healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reorienting health services. In a village this may mean clean water, safe paths, a support group and school access, not only exercise sheets.

sections.heading: Primary care systems
sections.text: Primary care is the first point of contact with the health system. Good primary care is accessible, continuous, comprehensive and coordinated. Physiotherapy supports it through advice, referral, training of community health workers and shared care plans. Case: after a stroke, Mr Okafor returns to a rural town. A community health worker checks his home, a relative helps him practise walking to the market, and the district physiotherapist reviews him monthly. The team records goals and refers him for eye care and social support. National plans differ, so check current local policy.

keyPoints: CBR combines health, education, livelihood, social and empowerment actions with community participation.
The ICF frames disability as functioning and participation shaped by body, activity, environment and personal factors.
Inclusion means removing barriers so people take part in school, work and community life.
Home programmes need training, supervision and review, not just a list of exercises.
Health promotion uses the Ottawa Charter areas, including supportive environments and community action.
Physiotherapy works in primary care through referral, advice, shared plans and training of community workers.

en.title: Assistive technology and mobility
en.short: Walking aids, wheelchairs, prostheses, orthoses and seating: assessment, fitting, training and maintenance.

sections.heading: Assessment and prescription
sections.text: Assistive technology is equipment that maintains or improves function. Common mobility aids include walking sticks, crutches, walkers and wheelchairs. Orthoses are external devices that support or correct a body part; prostheses replace a missing body part. User-centred prescription starts with the person’s goals, body function, home and community environment, and available support. Assess balance, strength, endurance, vision, cognition, skin and transfer ability. A device that is not matched to the user can cause falls, pain or pressure injury. Check current national or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance for products and referral pathways. Case: Amina, a student in Kano with a below-knee amputation, needs a prosthesis for campus. Her goals, limb health, socket fit, gait and cost are assessed with her.

sections.heading: Walking aids and wheelchairs
sections.text: Walking aids widen the base or share load. A stick is held opposite the affected side for hip or knee pain. Crutches need good balance and arm strength; a walker gives most stability but is slow. Fit matters: handgrip at wrist crease when standing, elbow slightly bent. Train on level ground, then stairs and kerbs as needed. Wheelchairs may be manual or powered. Prescribe by seat width, depth, height, support and pressure relief. A cushion reduces pressure injury risk but does not replace repositioning. Train wheelies, braking and transfers only with supervision. Maintenance includes tyres, brakes, fasteners and cushions.

sections.heading: Orthoses, prostheses and seating
sections.text: Orthoses include foot orthoses, ankle-foot orthoses and spinal braces. They support alignment, control movement or reduce pain. Check skin, circulation and fit soon after issue and at review. Prostheses need a well-fitting socket, suspension, alignment and gait training. Seating for people with poor trunk control or reduced sensation needs pressure distribution, trunk support and postural alignment. A seating assessment considers sitting tolerance, transfers, pressure areas and the chair’s use at home, school or work. Training and follow-up are part of the prescription. Users and carers should know daily checks, cleaning, when to return, and whom to contact. Replace or repair worn parts promptly.

keyPoints: Assistive technology is chosen with the user, based on goals, body function and environment.
Walking aids share load or widen support; fit and training reduce falls.
Wheelchair prescription includes seat dimensions, posture support and pressure relief.
Orthoses support or correct; prostheses replace a missing part and need socket fit and gait training.
Seating must protect skin and support posture, with regular pressure relief.
Training, maintenance and follow-up are essential parts of prescription; check current WHO and national guidance.

en.title: Professional ethics and law in physiotherapy
en.short: Consent, confidentiality, boundaries, scope, regulation, malpractice and vulnerable patients.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text: Ethics is the study of right conduct; law is the rules a country enforces. Physiotherapy ethics rests on respect for autonomy, doing good, avoiding harm and fairness. Valid consent must be voluntary, informed and given by someone with capacity. Capacity is decision-specific: assess whether the person can understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision. Children and adults who lack capacity are covered by national law, which varies. Confidentiality means keeping health information private. Share it only with consent, for the patient’s care on a need-to-know basis, or when the law or a clear public interest requires disclosure.

sections.heading: Boundaries and scope
sections.text: Professional boundaries protect patients from the power imbalance between therapist and patient. Avoid sexual or romantic relationships, financial exploitation and confusing dual roles. Scope of practice is the range of tasks your training, registration and employer authorise. Work within your competence and refer when unsure. Regulation is through a national board or council that sets registration, standards and discipline; professional associations add codes. Malpractice usually requires a duty of care, a breach of that duty, causation and harm, but the legal test differs by country.

sections.heading: Vulnerable patients
sections.text: Vulnerable patients include children, older people, people with cognitive impairment or disability, and those facing poverty, abuse or language barriers. Safeguarding means recognising risk and reporting it under local policy. Example: a physiotherapist treating a man with early dementia who refuses exercise should not simply accept a relative’s consent. The therapist assesses capacity for that decision, supports communication, and follows national law on best interests and family involvement. The therapist records the discussion.

sections.heading: Check current rules
sections.text: Law and codes change and differ between countries. In Nigeria, the Medical Rehabilitation Therapists (Registration) Board regulates physiotherapists; in the UK, the Health and Care Professions Council does. Check your current national law, regulator code, employer policy and, where relevant, World Health Organization guidance. This summary is education, not legal advice.

keyPoints: Valid consent must be voluntary, informed and given by a patient with capacity.
Capacity is decision-specific; follow national law for children and adults who lack it.
Keep information confidential and share it only with consent, need-to-know care, or when the law or a clear public interest requires it.
Maintain professional boundaries and work only within your competence and authorised scope.
Malpractice generally requires duty, breach, causation and harm, but tests vary by country.
Check current national law, regulator code and employer policy because rules differ.

en.title: Research methods and evidence-based physiotherapy
en.short: Research designs, measurement, critical appraisal, searching evidence and applying it safely in physiotherapy.

sections.heading: Designs and questions
sections.text: Evidence-based practice (EBP) means combining the best available research with clinical expertise and the patient’s values. Start with a focused question, often in PICO form: population, intervention, comparison and outcome. The design must fit the question. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) test interventions; cohort studies follow groups over time; case-control studies compare people with and without an outcome; cross-sectional studies measure one point in time. Systematic reviews combine studies in a structured way and are strongest when done well. A case series or expert opinion is weak evidence for cause and effect.

sections.heading: Measurement and appraisal
sections.text: Measurement has three key properties. Validity is whether a test measures what it claims. Reliability is whether repeated measurements agree. Responsiveness is the ability to detect change. For diagnostic tests, sensitivity is the proportion with the condition who test positive; specificity is the proportion without it who test negative. Example: in 100 people, 40 have a condition. The test is positive in 30 of them and in 12 of the 60 without it. Sensitivity is 30 ÷ 40 = 75%. Specificity is 48 ÷ 60 = 80%. Predictive values depend on prevalence, so they differ between settings. Critical appraisal checks risk of bias, confounding, blinding, intention-to-treat analysis (analysing patients in the groups they were assigned to) and confidence intervals.

sections.heading: Searching and applying
sections.text: Search PubMed, the Cochrane Library and PEDro, the physiotherapy evidence database, using PICO terms and synonyms. Record the date, terms and results. Read guidelines with care: check the date, country, target population, strength of recommendations and conflicts of interest. GRADE, a widely used rating system, separates certainty of evidence from strength of recommendation. Apply evidence to the person in front of you, considering values, resources and setting. Avoid overclaiming: a statistically significant result may be clinically small, below the minimal important difference, the smallest change patients see as worthwhile. Report absolute effects and confidence intervals, not only p values. If evidence is uncertain, say so and point to current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: EBP combines research evidence, clinical expertise and patient values.
PICO frames a searchable question: population, intervention, comparison, outcome.
Sensitivity = true positives ÷ people with the condition; specificity = true negatives ÷ people without it.
Predictive values change with prevalence, so a test can perform differently in another setting.
Critical appraisal checks risk of bias, confounding and confidence intervals, not just statistical significance.
Guidelines must be checked for date, country, population and strength of recommendation before use.

en.title: Advanced musculoskeletal rehabilitation
en.short: Complex musculoskeletal pain, tendinopathy, osteoarthritis, spine care and post-operative exercise progression.

sections.heading: Assessment and reasoning
sections.text: Advanced musculoskeletal rehabilitation begins with a biopsychosocial assessment (body, mind and social factors). Take a detailed history, screen for red flags (warning signs such as fracture, infection, cancer or cauda equina features), and measure pain, function and participation with patient-reported outcome measures.
