Record baseline range of motion, strength and function. Clinical reasoning weighs tissue, psychological and social factors. Post-operative assessment also checks wound healing, swelling, neurovascular status and the surgeon’s precautions. Guidelines differ between countries, so follow local protocols.

sections.heading: Tendinopathy and osteoarthritis
sections.text: Tendinopathy is persistent tendon pain and reduced function under load. Management centres on progressive loading: isometric (static) or slow resistance work first, then heavier resistance and spring-like exercises as pain allows. Passive treatments alone are insufficient. Osteoarthritis is joint degeneration with pain and stiffness. Exercise, education and weight management are core; surgery is selected for some people. Evidence supports exercise but effects are modest, so goals must be discussed. For example, Amina, 58, has knee osteoarthritis. A programme starts with quadriceps strengthening and walking, then adds stairs and sit-to-stand practice.

sections.heading: Spine care and surgery
sections.text: Spine care starts with screening and reassurance. Most low back pain is nonspecific; avoid unnecessary imaging and bed rest. Use education, graded activity and exercise, and address fear of movement. Post-operative rehabilitation is criterion-based (guided by clinical criteria): protect healing tissue, restore movement, then strength and function. Progression depends on pain, swelling, range and task quality, not time alone. For example, after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, Chidi walks and bears weight early as tolerated, then advances from knee extension and quadriceps activation to heavier weight-bearing loading when swelling is controlled and the surgeon permits.

sections.heading: Critical evidence use
sections.text: Critical use of evidence means asking whether a trial matches your patient, whether outcomes and effects are clinically worthwhile. Prefer systematic reviews and current guidelines, and check their date and setting. Record outcome measures to judge progress. Shared decision-making respects the person’s goals. National and WHO guidance change, so verify the current version rather than copying a protocol. This is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: Complex musculoskeletal pain needs biopsychosocial assessment and red flag screening.
Tendinopathy is managed mainly with progressive loading, not passive treatment alone.
Exercise, education and weight management are core for osteoarthritis.
Most low back pain is nonspecific; avoid unnecessary imaging and bed rest.
Post-operative progression should be criterion-based and follow the surgeon’s precautions.
Appraise current guidelines and use outcome measures with shared decision-making.

en.title: Advanced neurorehabilitation
en.short: Neuroplasticity, intensive task practice, technology-assisted therapy and outcome measurement in complex disability.

sections.heading: Neuroplasticity and principles
sections.text: Neuroplasticity is the nervous system’s ability to change its structure and function with experience. After injury, change depends on use: practised tasks strengthen connections, while disuse weakens them. Advanced practice applies principles such as salience (the task is meaningful to the person), repetition, intensity, task specificity and feedback. Intensity means more repetitions and effort, but it must be safe. Fatigue, pain, falls and cardiovascular risk need screening. Recovery and compensation differ: recovery restores impaired function, compensation uses another strategy. Both can be valid goals.

sections.heading: Task-specific and intensive training
sections.text: Task-specific training practises the actual activity the person wants to do, such as standing, reaching or walking, rather than isolated movements alone. It is broken into achievable steps and progressed as ability improves. Intensive training means many repetitions within a session and across weeks. Evidence supports intensive task practice for walking and arm function after stroke, but the best dose is uncertain and varies with the person. A case: Amina, after stroke, wants to carry a tray. Her therapist practises reaching, grasping and stepping with a tray, starting with five repetitions and building tolerance. Progress is reviewed, not assumed.

sections.heading: Technology and measurement
sections.text: Technology-assisted therapy includes treadmill or body-weight support gait training, robotics, virtual reality and telerehabilitation. It can increase repetitions and give immediate feedback, but it is an adjunct, not a replacement for skilled therapy. Check suitability, safety and cost. Outcome measurement uses valid, reliable tools at body-function and activity levels, such as the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for the upper limb, the Berg Balance Scale, the Functional Independence Measure and Goal Attainment Scaling. Measure before and after, and interpret change against published minimal important difference where available. Guidelines differ by country; follow current national and WHO rehabilitation guidance.

keyPoints: Neuroplasticity is experience-dependent: practice and use drive change.
Task-specific training practises the real activity the person wants to do.
Intensity means more repetitions and effort, but safety must be screened.
Technology can increase practice and feedback but does not replace skilled therapy.
Use valid and reliable outcome measures before and after intervention.
Guidelines differ by country; check current national and WHO guidance.

en.title: Advanced cardiorespiratory rehabilitation
en.short: Exercise physiology, prescription, monitoring and safety in cardiac, pulmonary and critical illness rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Physiology and goals
sections.text:
Advanced cardiorespiratory rehabilitation applies exercise physiology to heart failure, coronary disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), interstitial lung disease and critical illness. Cardiac rehabilitation combines exercise, education and risk-factor care; pulmonary rehabilitation combines supervised exercise, breathing training and self-management.

In critical illness, bed rest causes rapid loss of muscle mass and function, so early mobilisation aims to limit weakness. Exercise capacity depends on oxygen delivery, ventilation, gas exchange and muscle metabolism. Training improves aerobic capacity by central and peripheral adaptations, but response is smaller in severe disease. Assessment uses tests such as the six-minute walk test and cardiopulmonary exercise testing.

sections.heading: Prescription and monitoring
sections.text:
Exercise prescription follows frequency, intensity, time and type. Intensity may be set from a symptom-limited test using heart rate reserve: target = resting heart rate + (percentage × (peak heart rate − resting heart rate)). For example, resting 70 bpm and peak 150 bpm give a reserve of 80. At 40 percent, target = 70 + (0.40 × 80) = 102 bpm; at 60 percent, 70 + (0.60 × 80) = 118 bpm. Use the range set by local guidelines.

Perceived exertion and dyspnoea scores guide intensity when heart rate is unreliable, for example with beta-blockers or atrial fibrillation. Monitor symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and rhythm. Stop for chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness or unsafe desaturation, following local criteria.

sections.heading: Safety and evidence
sections.text:
Safety depends on screening, supervision and an emergency plan. Exercise should be individualised after medical assessment. In pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental oxygen may be used during exercise; physiotherapists generally do not adjust drug doses. Evidence supports supervised cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation for improving exercise capacity and quality of life, and early mobilisation in critical care for improving recovery of strength and function.

Guidelines differ by country and change, so check current national guidance or World Health Organization resources. Record baseline and outcomes. A small case: a patient with COPD completes pulmonary rehabilitation with interval walking, monitoring oxygen saturation and breathlessness, and reports less breathlessness on daily activities.

keyPoints: Cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation combine supervised exercise with education and self-management.
Critical illness causes rapid functional loss, so early mobilisation is a key rehabilitation aim.
Prescription uses frequency, intensity, time and type, individualised after assessment.
Heart rate reserve target = resting heart rate + (intensity fraction × (peak heart rate − resting heart rate)).
Use perceived exertion, symptoms and oxygen saturation when heart rate is unreliable.
Check current national or WHO guidance and local safety criteria, and do not adjust drug doses.

en.title: Research methods for a physiotherapy dissertation
en.short: Designing a physiotherapy dissertation: questions, methods, statistics, ethics, data management and writing.

sections.heading: Question design
sections.text: A dissertation question must be specific, answerable and ethical. For an effectiveness question, PICO helps: Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome. For an experience question, a broader qualitative question is better. A clear question sets the design, sample and analysis.

sections.heading: Methods and statistics
sections.text:
Quantitative methods include randomised controlled trials, cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies. They measure variables with valid and reliable outcome measures. Qualitative methods include interviews, focus groups and observation, often with purposive sampling and thematic analysis. Trustworthiness comes from triangulation, an audit trail and reflexivity, which means examining the researcher’s influence.

Statistics has two jobs: describe the sample and draw conclusions from data. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p values. A p value is the probability of results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true. Worked example: if 50 participants improve by a mean of 8 points with SD 10, the standard error is 10 ÷ √50 = 1.41. The approximate 95% confidence interval is 8 ± 1.96 × 1.41, or 5.2 to 10.8 points.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text: Ethics approval from a research ethics committee (sometimes called an institutional review board) is needed before recruitment. Informed consent must be voluntary, and participants need the right to withdraw. Physiotherapy research often involves patients, so protect privacy, anonymise data and store it securely. Data protection law and retention rules differ by country, so check current national and institutional guidance. A data management plan should say who can access data, how long it is kept and how it will be destroyed.

sections.heading: Writing up
sections.text: Scientific writing usually follows IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. Follow the reporting guideline for your design, such as CONSORT for trials, STROBE for observational studies and COREQ for qualitative work. State limitations honestly, avoid plagiarism and use the required referencing style. Write early, keep a methods diary and check the current guidance of your institution.

keyPoints: A good dissertation question is specific, answerable and ethical; PICO frames effectiveness questions.
Quantitative methods test hypotheses with numbers, while qualitative methods explore experience and meaning.
Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p values.
For a mean, standard error = SD ÷ √n and approximate 95% confidence interval = mean ± 1.96 × standard error.
Get ethics approval before recruitment and manage data securely under local law and institutional policy.
Write in IMRaD structure and follow the reporting guideline for your design.
